parts.title: Booking a Wildlife Boat Trip
parts.scenario: A man phones a boat company in a seaside town to find out about its wildlife-watching trips and book one for his family.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Fiona
voices.desc: Booking assistant at the boat company — female, 40s, bright, efficient and chatty; British accent (light northern English)

voices.label: Daniel
voices.desc: Caller — male, late 30s, friendly, slightly hurried, a father organising a family holiday; British accent (southern English)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a company to book a wildlife-watching boat trip. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 6.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [telephone rings twice, then the line clicks open] [bright, professional] Good morning, Calderwick Wildlife Cruises, Fiona speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [friendly, slightly hurried] Oh, hello. I'm hoping to book a boat trip for my family next month. We're coming up on holiday. But, um, I have to say I found your website a bit confusing. There seem to be quite a lot of different trips.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [warm, light laugh] You're not the first person to tell me that. It's being redesigned at the moment. Shall I just run through the options for you?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [relieved] That would be brilliant, thanks.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [clear, explaining] Right. The shortest one is what we call the Harbour Trip. That lasts an hour and a quarter, and it goes round the bay and then out to the sandbanks at the mouth of the river.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [interested] And what would we see on that one? My kids are desperate to see dolphins.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [gently honest] Well, I wouldn't book the Harbour Trip for dolphins, I'm afraid. They tend to stay much further out to sea. [brightening] What it is good for is seals. There's a colony of about two hundred that come out of the water onto the sandbanks, and the boat can get surprisingly close.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [pleased] Oh, they'd love that. And where does it go from? Is it the harbour steps? That's where we went from last time, but that was years ago.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [apologetic] It used to be, yes, but the steps were badly damaged in a storm last winter, so all our boats leave from the floating jetty now. That's on the opposite side of the harbour from the fish market, right next to the aquarium.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [repeating slowly, as if writing it down] The jetty... next to the aquarium. Okay. And how much is the Harbour Trip?

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [reading from a screen] For adults it's sixteen pounds fifty... [short pause] [correcting herself, a little flustered] oh, no, hang on, sorry, I've got last year's price list up. It's eighteen pounds fifty now. And children under fourteen pay half.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [good-humoured sigh] Eighteen fifty. Fair enough. What about the longer trips?

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [enthusiastic] So the one most families go for is the Island Trip. That goes out to Ravenholm Island. Now, the website still says it's a five-hour trip, but we've shortened it this season, so it's four hours altogether, and that includes your time on the island.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [doubtful] Four hours. Hmm. Is that going to be too long for a seven-year-old, do you think?

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [reassuring] Honestly, most children cope fine, because they get off the boat halfway through. [informative] The island's best known for its puffins, of course, and you'll almost certainly see gannets as well, diving for fish. [slightly wistful] There used to be a big colony of terns out there too, but they haven't nested on the island for three or four years now.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [thinking aloud] Puffins and gannets. Right. And what is there to actually do once you're on the island?

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [explaining] You get about forty-five minutes ashore. There's a little medieval chapel, but that's shut while the roof's being repaired, so I'd walk up to the lighthouse. There's a small exhibition inside, and the view from the top is wonderful.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [interested] Sounds great. And the price of that one?

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [matter-of-fact] It's forty-two pounds per adult, and that includes the landing fee for the island.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [hesitant] Okay. And is there anything in the evenings? My wife mentioned something about a sunset trip.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [helpful] Yes, that's the Evening Cruise. It's two hours, and it heads out to where the dolphins feed. [carefully] Now, we can't promise you'll see them. On average it's about two evenings out of three. But if dolphins are the priority, that's your best chance. It's thirty-five pounds.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [weighing it up, then decisive] Hmm. I think the Island Trip, then. The children are mad about puffins anyway, and we could always try the evening one another year.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [pleased] Lovely. Let me just take a few details from you.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 7 to 10.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [efficient] So, which date were you thinking of?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [checking a calendar] We arrive on the twentieth of August, so... the Saturday would be ideal. That's the twenty-second.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [typing, then apologetic] Ah. I'm really sorry, the Island Trip on the twenty-second is completely full. I could do the following day, if that's any good?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [thinking for a second] Sunday the twenty-third, then. Yes, that works fine, actually.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [brisk] Great. And can I take your name?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: It's Daniel Pellow. [slowly, spelling each letter clearly] That's P... E... double L... O... W.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [reading back as she types] B... E...

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [politely correcting her] No, sorry, it's P. P for Peter.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [light laugh] Sorry about that. P... E... double L... O... W. Got it. And that's two adults and two children?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That's right. The children are seven and eleven.

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [practical] Lovely. Now, on the day, you check in at the little ticket kiosk on the jetty. We used to ask people to turn up ten minutes before departure, but there's a safety briefing on the island boat now, with the lifejackets and so on, so please make sure you're there twenty minutes before it sets off.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [noting it down] Twenty minutes. Fine. And what's the best thing to do about parking? Is there a car park near the jetty?

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [explaining] There's one right by the beach, but it's very expensive in August. And the supermarket car park is closer, but you can only stay there for two hours, which is no good for a four-hour trip. [brightly] What I'd suggest is the car park behind the library. If you show your boat tickets to the attendant, there's no charge at all.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [pleased] Oh, that's handy. Thanks. And should we bring food?

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [friendly] There's no café on the island, so I'd bring a packed lunch. And warm clothes, even if it's sunny when you set off. It's always a good few degrees colder out at sea.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [chuckles] Noted. Right, shall I pay now?

script.speaker: Fiona
script.text: [cheerful] Yes, please. I'll just put you through to the payment line.

parts.title: Changes to Ashbury Market
parts.context: Monologue in an everyday social context (local radio talk, with a short host introduction)
parts.scenario: On a local radio programme, the town-centre manager explains why the town's outdoor market is being reorganised and describes the new layout of the market square.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Host
voices.desc: Local radio presenter — male, 50s, warm and upbeat; British accent

voices.label: Helen
voices.desc: Town-centre manager — female, 40s, confident, candid and well organised; British accent (Midlands)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a town-centre manager talking on local radio about changes to the town's market. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 16.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: [radio studio, a short jingle fading out] [warm, upbeat] And as promised, I'm joined in the studio by Helen Marsh, Ashbury's town-centre manager, to talk about the changes coming to our market. Helen, welcome.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [friendly, confident] Thanks, Jim. It's good to be here. [measured] I'm sure a lot of your listeners have heard that the market's being reorganised from April, and I'd like to explain why, and what it's actually going to mean for people.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [candid, firm] Let me deal with one rumour straight away. People keep telling me this is all happening because the market's losing traders. That simply isn't the case. We've got more stallholders now than we had five years ago, and there's a waiting list for pitches.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [explaining] What really started this off was a questionnaire we ran last spring. Over two thousand people filled it in, and the clearest message was that anyone working nine to five felt the market was never open when they could get to it. They were asking us, quite simply, to stay open later into the day.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [more serious] The other issue, frankly, was safety. At the moment the stalls run down both sides of Bridge Street, and delivery lorries are still squeezing between them first thing in the morning. We've had two or three near misses with pedestrians this year, and that can't go on.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [even-handed] Now, some of the shopkeepers on the High Street have complained that the stalls hide their windows, and I do understand that. But to be fair, that complaint's been made for decades, and it isn't what's driving the changes. And yes, the old canvas canopies are being replaced, but that's being funded by a regional grant. It's a separate project, not a reason for the move.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [clear, moving on] So, what's changing? First, the Thursday market. Some people assumed we'd move it to Wednesday, and we did look at that, but Wednesday's when the farmers' market runs over in Hexton, and we'd just be competing with them. [reassuring] So Thursday stays Thursday, and the opening hours won't change either.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [explaining] What will be different is what's on sale. From April, Thursdays will be given over entirely to food: fruit and veg, cheese, bread, fish and so on. The clothing and household stalls will move to Saturdays instead, when there's more room.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [sympathetic] I know a lot of traders have been worried about rents. We had originally planned a small increase for everybody to help cover the new canopies, but once the grant came through, there was no need for it. [firm, clear] So for the first twelve months, every trader will pay exactly what they're paying now, and we'll review it after that.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [measured] Some traders have also asked for a discount if they sign up for two years rather than one. That's something we're looking at, but no decision's been made yet, so please don't take it as a promise.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [warmer, enthusiastic] Now, the evening market, which is the really new thing. Our first idea was to hold it every Friday all year round, but the traders pointed out, quite rightly, that hardly anyone's going to stand about in the dark in January. And just once a month didn't seem enough to build up a regular crowd. So it'll be every Friday from May until the end of September, from five till nine.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [apologetic, practical] Parking is the question I get asked most. I'm afraid there's no room to create extra spaces anywhere near the square. We also looked at running a park-and-ride bus from the retail park, but the figures just didn't add up. [brighter] What we have agreed with the council is that the multi-storey on Station Road won't charge for the first two hours on any market day.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 17 to 20.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: [curious] And Helen, the stalls are all coming off Bridge Street and into the Market Square itself. Can you describe how it'll be laid out?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [clear, guiding] Of course. Imagine you're standing on the steps of the Town Hall, looking out over the square. The fountain's in the middle in front of you, the High Street runs along the far side, and Church Street comes in on your right.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [explaining] The hot food stalls were the hardest to place. We'd thought about the corner just to your left, beside the Town Hall, but the council offices are right there and nobody wanted cooking smells drifting in. So they'll be in the far left-hand corner, where Bridge Street meets the High Street. That's handy for people coming over the bridge, too.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [informative] The flower stalls need shade, so they won't be out in the open in the corner nearest the High Street on your right. Instead they'll be halfway down the right-hand side of the square, exactly where Church Street comes in, because the church wall keeps the sun off them for most of the day.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [clarifying] The information point is moving too. It used to be in front of the fountain, on the High Street side. From April, you'll find it right beside the fountain, on its left-hand side as you look from the Town Hall steps, so it's the first thing you see if you come in from Bridge Street.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [warm] And finally, we're adding a seating area with benches and some planters. We'd hoped to put that on the left-hand side, beside the bank, but the bank needs that space kept clear for the queue at its cash machines. So the seating will go in the corner just to your right as you come down the Town Hall steps, at the end of the building, which is lovely and sunny in the afternoon.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: [cheerful, wrapping up] Sounds great. Helen Marsh, thank you very much.

options.A: a fall in the number of people running stalls
options.B: objections from owners of nearby shops
options.C: a demand for the market to operate at different times
options.D: a risk of accidents in the current location
options.E: the poor condition of the market's equipment

The other issue, frankly, was safety

question_groups.layout: A rectangular Market Square, wider east–west than north–south. The TOWN HALL fills the north side, with its STEPS in the middle of its south face, leading down into the square (the listener stands on these steps facing south). A BANK (labelled, with cash machines) stands on the east side of the square, halfway along. COUNCIL OFFICES are labelled at the east end of the Town Hall. G = between the fountain and the High Street (directly south of the fountain). H = south-east corner, where Bridge Street meets the High Street.

parts.title: The Economics of Music Streaming
parts.scenario: Two business students discuss their project on the economics of music streaming with their tutor.
parts.accent: Tutor British (en-GB); Maya American (en-US); Callum British (en-GB)

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Dr Hughes
voices.desc: Tutor — female, 50s, precise, encouraging but probing; British RP accent

voices.label: Maya
voices.desc: Student — female, early 20s, energetic, quick to form opinions; American accent (en-US)

voices.label: Callum
voices.desc: Student — male, early 20s, cautious, analytical, slightly dry humour; British accent (Scottish-influenced)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Maya and Callum, talking to their tutor about their project on the economics of music streaming. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [office, a door closing softly] [warm, businesslike] Come in, both of you. So, how's the streaming project going? You're about halfway through now, aren't you?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: [energetic] Yeah, just about. And honestly, it's been kind of eye-opening.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [interested] In what way? What's struck you most so far?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: [thinking aloud] Well, I went in expecting the big story to be how differently the platforms pay per stream. And they do vary, but it's a fraction of a cent either way, so that wasn't really the headline.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [dry] And everyone keeps telling us that vinyl's making a comeback, but I'd read loads about that before we started, so it was hardly news to me.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [curious] Not the gap between the top artists and everyone else?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: [light laugh] No, we kind of knew that going in. The top one percent taking most of the money is no secret.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: [emphatic] What neither of us had expected was that the streaming companies themselves are barely making any money. Most of them have run at a loss for years. We'd both assumed they were the ones getting rich.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [knowingly] Yes, that surprises a lot of people. Now, your original plan was to compare artists' contracts across different record labels. You've moved away from that, I gather?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [slightly rueful] We have. It wasn't that the topic had been done to death. There's quite a bit written on it, but we could've found a new angle. [sighs] The problem was that none of the labels would let us see the actual figures. Every contract we asked about was confidential.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [measured] I did warn you it was ambitious, but I wouldn't have told you to drop it. It just wasn't going to work without the numbers. Fair enough. So, you've done some interviews instead. How many?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: Eight. Mostly local musicians, plus a couple of people from small labels.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [thoughtful, probing] Eight's perfectly adequate for a project of this scale, so the number doesn't worry me. And I'm glad you recorded them all. [more critical] What does concern me is the way a few of the questions were worded. Asking someone, 'Don't you feel you're underpaid?' rather invites them to agree with you.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [conceding, a little embarrassed] Yeah, that's fair. That one was mine.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: [keen, moving on] Can we talk about the user-centric model? Where your subscription only goes to the artists you actually listen to, rather than into one big pool. I think it'd be so much fairer, especially for niche artists, like jazz or folk musicians, whose fans pay but whose money ends up with the big pop stars.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [sceptical, careful] I'm not so sure. The studies we've read suggest it would shift income by a few percent at most. For the vast majority of musicians, I really don't think it would change much at all.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [even-handed] The platforms also argue it would be expensive to run, though I suspect they've exaggerated that. Anyway, you can present both views. And for the presentation itself?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: [enthusiastic] I wanted to do a live demo of the royalty calculator we built, but...

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [interrupting, wry] But the Wi-Fi in that seminar room is a nightmare, so that's out.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [gently] And please don't add any more comparison charts. Your draft slides already have far too many. What would really bring it to life is something more concrete.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [decisive] Then let's follow one local band's earnings over a year, from start to finish. We've got the data from the Harbour Lights interview.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: [agreeing] Okay, yeah. Let's go with that.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [businesslike] Right. Now, in the findings section, you look at different groups in the industry. Talk me through them.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: [organised] Sure. We started with the major labels. You'd expect their streaming money to come from whatever's in the charts right now, but it doesn't. Something like seventy percent comes from recordings that are more than eighteen months old. A lot of it's music from the eighties and nineties.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [probing] And why is that, do you think?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [thoughtful] Partly the recommendation algorithms, which keep suggesting familiar songs. And older listeners have finally moved over to streaming, so they're playing what they grew up with.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [adding] And people assume they've got all the power in negotiations with the platforms. We'd question that, actually. The platforms need them, but they need the platforms just as much now.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: Interesting. What about songwriters?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [explaining carefully] I'd assumed streaming would be their biggest earner, but for most of them it isn't. Radio and TV licensing still bring in more. The real finding, though, was that huge sums never reach them, because the information attached to each track, the writers' names and so on, is so often missing or wrong. So the money can't be matched to anyone.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [serious] Yes, that's a well-documented problem. And session musicians?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: [a little indignant] That's the one that really got to me. You'd think they'd make up for it by selling T-shirts and things, but they can't, because they're not the face of the band. They're paid a one-off fee for the recording, and that's it. However many millions of times the track's streamed, they don't get another penny.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [quietly] A couple of musicians' unions are campaigning to change that, but nothing's been agreed so far.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [thoughtful] Mm. And the independent labels?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [considering] Some of them sell merchandise, but they always have, so that's nothing new. What has changed is that, by joining together through a few big distributors, they can now negotiate with the platforms on much better terms than they could ten years ago.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: [slightly doubtful] I'm not sure that applies to the really small ones, but, yeah, overall that's what the evidence shows.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [encouraging] Fine, just acknowledge that. And the last group, the concert promoters?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: [lively] They're actually doing pretty well out of it. They don't earn anything from streams directly. [short pause] But they look at where an artist's listeners are concentrated, city by city, and use that to decide where to book a tour.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [amused] So they profit from streaming without being paid for it.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: Exactly. Not from it, but because of it.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [light laugh] Which is a bit ironic, given how little the artists earn from the streams themselves.

script.speaker: Dr Hughes
script.text: [wrapping up, approving] It is. Well, this is all coming together nicely. Get the revised slides to me by Friday, and we'll go through them next week.

parts.title: Animal Camouflage
parts.scenario: A zoology lecturer explains the main forms of animal camouflage, including background matching, disruptive colouration and counter-shading, and their costs.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Lecturer
voices.desc: Zoology lecturer — male, 50s, articulate, lively, occasionally dry; British RP accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about animal camouflage. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lecture theatre, faint murmur fading] [lively, clear] Good morning, everyone. Today we're looking at camouflage: the ways in which animals avoid being detected, or recognised, by predators, or indeed by their prey. It's a field that's changed a great deal in the last twenty years, largely because researchers have started to test ideas experimentally rather than simply describing what they see.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] The simplest strategy is known as background matching, where an animal's colour and pattern resemble its surroundings. A stick insect on a twig, a sandy-coloured lizard on a dune. [explaining] Some species go further, and change their appearance as their surroundings change. The ptarmigan, a bird of mountain and tundra regions, is brown in summer and pure white in winter.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [emphatic, slowing down] Now, you'd naturally assume that it's falling temperatures that trigger the change. They don't. Birds kept in warm conditions still turn white on schedule. What sets off the moult is the shortening of the daylight in autumn, which is a far more reliable signal of the season than the weather.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] Of course, a moult takes weeks. Other animals can change far more quickly. Flatfish such as the plaice, lying on the seabed, adjust both the shade and the pattern of their skin to match the sand or gravel beneath them. [wry] It was once believed this took hours. In fact, filmed experiments show that most of the change happens within seconds.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [aside, slightly amused] You may be wondering why I haven't mentioned the chameleon. The popular idea is that it changes colour to blend in, but that's largely a myth. Its rapid colour changes are mainly signals, to rivals or potential mates, so if anything they make the animal more noticeable, not less.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [shifting, clear] The second strategy is disruptive colouration. Here the markings don't so much match the background as break up the animal's outline. Bold, high-contrast patches create false edges, so a predator's visual system fails to see the separate parts of the body as belonging to a single animal.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining carefully] An important detail is where these markings are placed. Patches in the centre of the body have relatively little effect. It's those that touch the edges of the body that do most to make the body impossible to recognise.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [engaged, storytelling] How do we know any of this actually works? Well, in a well-known series of field experiments, researchers pinned artificial 'moths' to tree trunks in woodland. You might picture solid plastic models, but these targets were triangles cut from paper and printed with different patterns, each with a dead mealworm attached as a reward. The researchers then counted how many mealworms were taken by birds.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [pleased] And the targets with disruptive markings survived significantly longer than those that merely matched the bark, particularly when the markings reached the edges of the triangle.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [moving on, clear] Which brings us to counter-shading. Many animals, from deer to sharks, are darker on their upper surface and paler underneath. The principle is often attributed to a zoologist, but it was in fact first described in the 1890s by an American painter, Abbott Thayer, which is why you'll sometimes see it called Thayer's Law.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining, with emphasis] The logic is this. When light comes from above, a uniformly coloured animal looks lit on its back and dark on its belly, and it's this graded shading that tells our brains we're looking at a solid, three-dimensional object. Counter-shading cancels out the shadow on the underside, so the body appears flat and much harder to pick out.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [intrigued] A nice confirmation of this comes from certain caterpillars that habitually rest upside down beneath twigs. In those species the pattern is reversed: they're paler on the back and darker on the belly. Exactly what you'd predict, since for them it's the belly that faces the light.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] In the sea, counter-shading does a slightly different job. Penguins and many fish are dark on their backs, so that from above they blend with the deep water below. But it's the pale belly that's more interesting. Seen from beneath, against the bright surface of the water, a dark belly would stand out as a clear silhouette. A pale one is far less visible.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [enthusiastic] One of the most striking recent findings comes from palaeontology. A remarkably well-preserved fossil of a small dinosaur, Psittacosaurus "/ˌsɪt.ə.koʊˈsɔː.rəs/", retained traces of its original pigment, and it clearly showed counter-shading.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [careful, analytical] What's more, the pattern of the shading can tell us about light conditions. Under direct sunlight in open country, the transition from dark to light on the body is quite sharp and set high up. On this animal, it was gradual and low down, which is what you'd expect under diffuse light. So the evidence points not to the open plains, as had been assumed, but to a forest habitat, with light filtered through a dense canopy.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [briefly] There are other strategies I'll only mention today: masquerade, where an animal resembles an object like a leaf or a bird dropping, and motion dazzle, the bold stripes that may make speed hard to judge. We'll come back to those next week.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [reflective] Finally, it's worth remembering that camouflage isn't free. People often suggest the main cost is the energy needed to produce pigments, but that's actually quite small. The real cost is behavioural. Camouflage only works if the animal stays motionless, so a well-hidden animal spends long periods unable to feed or look for a mate.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [practical, wrapping up] And it ties animals to particular places. A white ptarmigan on a hillside where the snow has melted early is very conspicuous indeed. [dry] With warming winters, that mismatch is becoming a real problem. Right, for next week, please read the two papers on the reading list.

items.evidence: by an American painter, Abbott Thayer

items.evidence: Counter-shading cancels out the shadow on the underside

items.evidence: but to a forest habitat, with light filtered through a dense canopy
